title: Ubi Primum (Leo XII), in The Encyclical Letter of Pope Leo the XII. ... with an English Translation of the Same (Dublin: Richard Coyne, 1824), "Translation", pp. 11–18

passages.text:
TRANSLATION.

TO OUR VENERABLE BRETHREN, PATRIARCHS, PRIMATES, ARCHBISHOPS, AND BISHOPS,

LEO THE XII. POPE,

Venerable Brethren, Health and the Apostolical Benediction.

As soon as we had been raised to the summit of the apostolic office, we cried out with St. Leo the Great, “Lord, I have heard thy report, and I feared; I have considered thy works, and I trembled; for what so strange, so terrifying, as labour to him who is weak, an exalted station to a lowly person, dignity to him who has no merit; and yet we do not despair nor do we fail, because we confide not in ourselves, but in Him who worketh in us.”

We desired, Venerable Brethren, to address you without delay, and to impart the sentiments of our heart to you,—to you indeed, who are our crown and our joy, and to whom, on that account, we hope that your own flocks are a crown and a consolation; but distracted as we have been, partly by the weighty cares of our apostolic ministry, and partly, nay chiefly, by the prolonged illness which has oppressed us, we have not, alas! been hitherto able to satisfy our desire. But God, rich in mercy, who bestows without bounds his gifts on those who petition and pray to him with confidence, and who hath inspired us with this desire, enables us at present to fulfil it. Nor was this our silence, though necessarily so much prolonged, without its consolation, for God, who consoles the humble, hath also consoled us by the religious affection of your devotion and zeal for us, in which we clearly discern the piety of Christian unity, so as the more to rejoice and give thanks to God. Hence, as a proof of our love, we write at present to you, that we may impart to you new incentives to run in the way of the divine com-

mandments, and to fight still more valiantly the battles of the Lord, that thus doing, the pastor may glory in the advancement of the flock.

You know, Venerable Brethren, that the apostle Peter instructed bishops in the following words: “Feed the flock of God, which is among you, taking care thereof not by constraint, but willingly, according to God; neither for the sake of filthy lucre, but voluntarily; neither as domineering over the clergy, but being made a pattern of the flock from the heart.” 

From this you will easily perceive what mode of proceeding is prescribed for you, what the virtues are which you should studiously cultivate, what abundance of learning should adorn your mind, and what the fruits of piety and love are, which you should not only bring forth in yourselves, but communicate also to your flocks. Thus truly you will attain the end of your ministry; thus, being a pattern of the flock from the heart, and distributing to some milk, to some strong food, you will not only by your doctrine, but also by your works and example, form the flock itself so as to enable them to lead here a quiet life in Christ Jesus, but you will also conduct them, together with yourselves, to eternal bliss: the same chief of the apostles declaring, “and when the Prince of pastors will appear, then will you receive an unfading crown of glory.”

We would wish to remind you of many things; we shall touch, however, only on a few, intending to treat hereafter of what is most important, according as these distressing times may require.

The things relating to those, who, with great caution, and after mature deliberation, are to be promoted to minor orders, and especially to holy orders, and which the Apostle has taught in the following words to Timothy, “do not hastily impose hands on any one,” the things appertaining to the appointment of pastors, having the care of souls in your dioceses respectively, as also to the establishment of seminaries of the Clergy, and which have been decreed in the Council of Trent, and afterwards more fully explained by our predecessors, all these are so well known to you, that there is no necessity to dwell more at length upon them.

You know, Venerable Brethren, how important, and how strictly to be observed, is that personal residence in your dioceses, to which you are bound by virtue of your office; this same appearing clearly from very many decrees of councils and apostolical constitutions, and being confirmed also by the most holy Council of Trent in these words: “Whereas

all to whom the care of souls has been committed, are obliged by a divine precept to know their flocks, to offer up sacrifice for them, and to feed them by the preaching of the word of God, the administration of the sacraments, and the example of every good work; to have a paternal care of the poor, and of other destitute persons, and to apply themselves to the other pastoral duties, all which things cannot be done or fulfilled by those who do not watch over and attend their flocks, but, like hirelings, abandon them. The most holy Synod admonishes and exhorts them, (the bishops,) that, mindful of the commands of God, and being made patterns of the flocks, they feed them and rule them in judgment and truth. We also, stricken with the obligation of so great and so weighty an office, and inflamed with zeal for the glory of God, heartily commend those who fulfil exactly this commandment; and if there be any (and that there should be some in so great a number of pastors is not surprising, though greatly to be lamented) who do not obey these ecclesiastical ordinances, the same we admonish, exhort, and beseech, through the bowels of the mercy of Jesus Christ, to reflect seriously that the sovereign Judge will require the blood of his sheep at their hands, and that a most rigorous judgment awaits those who rule.

The foregoing terrific sentence, as you well know, applies not only to those who neglect to reside personally, or who seek to evade it by some vain pretext, but also to those who, without a just cause, neglect to undergo the labour of a visitation, and the fulfilling of it as prescribed by the canons. They truly will not comply with the decree of Trent, unless they take care to come in person to their sheep, and, like a good shepherd, to cherish the good, to seek after those who have strayed, and by calling and tending them, whether sweetly or vigorously, to bring them back at length to the fold.

Those bishops, moreover, who do not endeavour with becoming zeal to obey the precepts which oblige them to reside and to visit, will not escape the terrible judgment of the supreme Pastor, our Saviour, by pleading that they have fulfilled these duties by fit ministers.

It is to themselves, not to deputies, that the care of their flocks has been committed; to them the peculiar grace of the Holy Ghost, to them the gifts of the choicest grace were promised. Hence it happens, that the sheep hear much more willingly the voice of the pastor, than of a substitute; and that they ask with more confidence, and more willingly receive, as from the hand of the Lord, whose person they venerate in their bishops, wholesome food from the hand of their own pastor, than from that of his vicar; all which, in addition to the proofs adduced, is confirmed by experience, that best mistress of things.

It would be sufficient, Venerable Brethren, to have written thus much to you; to you I say, who, though silent, are not ungrateful for the gifts you have received, and who are not proud, presuming on your own merits. Such, truly, it becometh those to be, who ardently desire to proceed from virtue to virtue, and still farther to advance, zealously copying after the examples of the holy prelates in ancient and modern times, and glorying in the Lord at having put to flight the enemies of the Church, and reformed the corrupted morals of men. But, nevertheless, let the golden saying of St. Leo the Great be ever present to your mind: “In this conflict no victory is so complete, as that after the triumph new contests will not arise.”

But how numerous and how severe are the contests which have arisen, and arise almost daily, against the Catholic Religion in these our times! Who thinking on them, and revolving them in his mind, can refrain from tears!

Attend closely, Venerable Brethren: that spark is not small of which St. Jerome speaks: “It is not, I say, a small spark which when seen is scarcely visible, but it is a flame which endeavours to lay waste almost the entire world, and to consume walls, cities, the most extensive plains and forests: the leaven is not small which appears to be so, but it is a leaven which, mixed with the meal, seeks to ferment the entire mass.” The lowliness of our apostolic ministry would fail through terror, only that “He does not sleep nor slumber who keepeth Israel,” and who says to his disciples, “Lo, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world,” and that he has vouchsafed to be not only the Guardian of the flock, but the Pastor also of the pastors themselves. But wherefore these remarks? A certain sect, not unknown certainly to you, usurping to itself undeservedly the name of Philosophy, has raked from the ashes disorderly crowds of almost every error. This sect, exhibiting a meek appearance of piety and liberality, professes Latitudinarianism or Indifferentism, (so it is called,) and extols it not only in civil matters, (of which we do not treat,) but also in religion, teaching that God has given free leave to every person to embrace or adopt, without any risk of his salvation, whatever sect is most pleasing to him, according to his own private judgment or opinion. Against which impiety of infatuated men, the apostle Paul thus admonishes us: “I beseech you, Brethren, to mark those who cause dissensions and offences contrary to the doctrine which you have learned, and avoid them: for they that are such serve not Christ our Lord, but their own belly, and by pleasing speeches and good words seduce the hearts of the innocent.”

Truly this error is not novel, but in these our times it is vaunted in a new and more insolent manner against the strength and integrity of the Catholic faith. Eusebius relates from Rhodon, that this insanity was broached in the second century by a heretic of the name of Apelles, who asserted that “faith was not to be at all inquired into, but that each person should remain in that which he had once imbibed;” whereas, as this Apelles affirmed, all those who hoped in Him who was crucified, would be saved, provided their works were found good. Rhetorius also, as Augustine testifies, foolishly asserted, that all heretics were in a safe way, and spoke truly; which, adds the holy father, is so absurd, as to appear to me incredible. But the present Indifferentism is known to have proceeded so far as insolently to contend, that not only all sects which are outside the Catholic Church, and which admit, at least in words, Revelation as their base and foundation, but that also those societies, who, despising Revelation, profess pure Deism or Naturalism, that all these walk uprightly. The Indifferentism of Rhetorius seemed, and justly, to St. Augustine an absurdity, and yet it was confined within certain limits; but the Latitudinarianism, which extends itself to Deism and Naturalism, which was rejected even by the ancient heretics, can this ever be approved of by any reasonable man? and yet, alas! in these times, it is approved of, commended, and defended, by men miscalled philosophers.

There have not been wanting, indeed, many excellent writers, professing a true philosophy, who assailed with irrefragable arguments this hideous monster; but it is a matter of itself so clear, that God, who is infinitely true—nay, who is truth itself, who rules all things with wisdom and goodness, and remunerates all who serve him—that it would be impossible for him to approve of all sects teaching doctrines false, and conflicting, and contradictory, and bestow everlasting rewards on those who profess them, is of itself so clear, as to render further observations upon it superfluous. We have, indeed, a more firm word of prophecy and writing to you. We speak wisdom amongst the perfect, not indeed the wisdom of this world, but the wisdom of God in mystery, by which we are taught, and with a divine faith believe in one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and that no other name under heaven is given to men besides the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, in which we can be saved; on which account also we profess that out of the Church there is no salvation.

But, oh! the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how incomprehensible are his judgments! God, who reproves the wisdom of the wise, seems to have given over the enemies of his Church, who despise Revelation, to a reprobate sense, and to that mystery of iniquity which was written on the forehead of the harlot, of whom mention is made by John; for truly, what iniquity can be more great than for these proud men not only to relinquish true religion, but also, by every kind of cavil, by speeches and writings full of guile, to seek to ensnare the incautious? Let God arise and check, restrain, and annihilate, this excessive licentiousness of speaking, writing, and publishing abroad!!

Shall we dwell further upon these subjects? The wickedness of our foes has proceeded so far, that in addition to a deluge of pernicious books, hostile to religion, they endeavour to employ to its detriment the sacred Scriptures, which were given to us by God for its support.

You are aware, Venerable Brethren, that a certain Society, commonly called the Bible Society, strolls with effrontery throughout the world; which Society, contemning the traditions of the Holy Fathers, and contrary to the well-known decree of the Council of Trent, labours with all its might, and by every means, to translate—or rather to pervert—the Holy Bible into the vulgar languages of every nation; from which proceeding, it is greatly to be feared that what is ascertained to have happened as to some passages, may also occur with regard to others; to wit: “that, by a perverse interpretation, the Gospel of Christ be turned into a human Gospel, or, what is still worse, into the Gospel of the Devil.”

To avert this plague, our predecessors published many ordinances; and in his latter days, Pius VII., of blessed memory, sent two Briefs—one to Ignatius, Archbishop of Gnesen, the other to Stanislaus, Archbishop of Mohilow—in which are many proofs, accurately and wisely collected from the sacred Scriptures and from tradition, to show how noxious this most wicked novelty is to both faith and morals.

We also, Venerable Brethren, in conformity with our apostolic duty, exhort you to turn away your flock, by all means, from these poisonous pastures. Reprove, beseech, be instant in season and out of season, in all patience and doctrine, that the faithful intrusted to you (adhering strictly to the rules of our congregation of the Index) be persuaded, that if the sacred Scriptures be every where indiscriminately published, more evil than advantage will arise thence, on account of the rashness of

men. Which truth is not only proved by experience, but St. Augustine, as well as the other Holy Fathers, has announced it in the following words: “For heresies have arisen, and certain perverse doctrines, ensnaring souls, and precipitating them into the abyss, have been broached only when the good Scriptures had been badly understood, and when that which was badly understood in them was rashly and boldly asserted.”

Behold then, Venerable Brethren, the tendency of this Society, which moreover, to attain its ends, leaves nothing untried; for not only does it print its translations, but also, wandering through the towns and cities, it delights in distributing them amongst the crowd. Nay, to allure the minds of the simple, at one time it sells them, at another, with an insidious liberality, it bestows them.

But if any person desire to ascertain the true source of all the evils which we have hitherto deplored, or of those which, lest we would be tedious, we have passed over, he will find, that, at the commencement of the Church, as well as now, it always originated in an obstinate contempt of the authority of the Church itself; yea, of that Church, which, as St. Leo the Great teaches by a charity the best regulated, contemplates Peter in the See of Peter, and in the person of the Roman Pontiff, his successor, looks to him, and honours him; in whom the care of all the pastors, together with the flocks committed to them, continues, and whose dignity does not fail even in his unworthy heir. In Peter therefore, (as the same holy Doctor wisely admonishes,) the strength of all is fortified, and the aid of divine grace is so regulated, that the firmness which Christ imparted to Peter, is communicated by Peter to the Apostles. It is likewise evident, that this contempt of the authority of the Church is opposed to the command of Christ, thus addressing the Apostles, and in their persons, the ministers of the Church succeeding to them: “Whosoever hears you, hears me; whosoever despises you, despises me.” And the admonition, also, of St. Paul, saying, “the Church, which is the pillar and the ground of truth;” which words Augustine, when considering, said: “If any one be found without the Church, he will be estranged from the number of the children; nor will he have God for his Father, who wills not to have the Church for his Mother.”

Do ye therefore, Venerable Brethren, place, with Augustine, the words of Christ and of the Apostle Paul before your eyes, and meditate frequently upon them, that you may teach the

people committed to you, how venerable the authority of the Church is, which has been settled immediately by God himself.

Be not disheartened. We acknowledge with the same Augustine, that these waters of the deluge (to wit, the multiplicity of different doctrines) press upon us at every side. We are not within the deluge, but we are encompassed by it; the waters approach us, but do not overwhelm us; they come near to us, but they do not ingulf us.”

Again, therefore, we exhort you, that your courage fail not. The power of temporal princes will, we trust in the Lord, come to your assistance, whose interest, as reason and experience show, is concerned when the authority of the Church is questioned; for it can never happen, that the things which are Cæsar’s would be given to Cæsar, if the things that are God’s be not given to God.

The duty of our servitude to you will also, to use the language of St. Leo, be present with you. In distress, in doubt, in every difficulty, have recourse to this Apostolic See, for God, as St. Augustine says, has placed in the Chair of unity the doctrine of Truth.

Lastly, we beseech you by the mercy of God, assist us by your desires and prayers, poured out to God, that the spirit of Grace may remain in us, and that your judgments may not fluctuate. And may He who has inspired you with the zeal of unanimity, grant to us all the gift of peace; that during all the days of our life, being devoted to the service of the Almighty God, and to yours, we may with confidence pray to the Lord, “Holy Father, keep them in thy Name, whom thou hast given to me.” As a pledge of which hope, and of our love, we impart, from our whole heart, to you and to your flocks, the Apostolical Benediction.

Given at Rome, at St. Mary Major’s, the 3rd day of May, 1824. The first year of our Pontificate.
